Orwell holds your hand so firmly throughout the entirety of the experience that it is almost hard to call it a game. The 1st mission you are given gives you hope of a grand experience of cyber sleuthing where you trawl through the lives of unaware citizens of the nation flagged up by your partner.  Then, you get to the rest of the game and realise that everything is still gloriously highlighted for you and that your only real task is ignoring irrelevant data and every now and then making a decision on certain conflicting datapoints.  It is the height of tedium and only the slow reveal the various charachters and their lives gives this any meaning.
This game tries to do the slow curtain pull that Horizon Zero Dawn did with absolutely none of the charm or charisma of that game.  2hrs in and along with my chances of a refund circling the drain is my level of interest in the conclusion of the story.  I will not come back to finish this none game, this thing that cannot even be described as a jigsaw given that not only are all the pieces highlighted for you, they are then put in place for you.  What is the point?
Orwell is yet another title that has all the potential in the world and delivers on none of it.
This game doesn't look like much from the video, but once you start playing it, you'll get hooked. There's so much do discover it's almost like reading a good book.
Basically an interactive novel with very little choice and on rails progression.
I was pleasantly suprised with Orwell. It really captivated my and I ended up playing the entire game in one sitting.
Buy it. Really really fun and good value for the price.

Orwell is a pretty interesting game, you feel quite immersed, almost like if you really is the character...

The soundtrack is great and contributes a lot to create a sense of drama at important moments, characters are well developed and the plot is overall pretty good, there are multiple endings and the choices are not always particularly clear, being the best investigator possible may not be of your interest at all times depending on how you'd like the game to end.

Overall, its a very interesting experience, I enjoyed it, my only observation is that at times you can come to conclusions that you have no way of uploading to Orwell, some facts may be pretty obvious, and still you can't act on them if you don't have a clear piece of datachunk to upload.

Anyway, good game, worthwhile, try it out!
Highly recommended!

I'll be honest, this one surprised me! And I actually had decent expectations to begin with. After playing the demo I figured it'd be a well done pick-your-own-adventure sort of deal, dressed up as something more intricate, but I'd say this went well beyond that. Simply put, the demo really is just a taste of what comes later. The game does a lot with the limited gameplay it has available. The story handles the subject matter fantastically and actually managed to surprise me (and it's quite a relevant tale these days). The final chapter was genuinely tense and left me constantly reconsidering my options. I'd have to play it again to see how much of the choices were an illusion, but it did feel like actions genuinely had large and unforeseen consequences. 

I have some small complaints, like I sometimes felt that I should be able to override the conflicting data chunks or felt stuck while the game waited for me to upload chunks for which I didn't feel I had enough justification to upload them, but some of that is part of the story and some of it is just the limitations of a narrative like this. Overall, they're fairly minor issues.

I can wholeheartedly recommend the game at full price and I'm looking forward to the sequel.

Orwell was an enjoyable, but very flawed game. I struggle with recommending it to anybody, because I can't imagine a particular audience falling in love with it. Gamers looking for a great narrative may find Orwell's offerings lacking, as I have. Gamers who are fans of the works of George Orwell may get what they're looking for, but as a fan myself I find the game's vision lacking. George Orwell's works were a denouncement of totalitarianism, yet his most well-known fictional books were either set in the real world or clearly based on real events and people. Orwell the game instead opts to take place in the wonderful setting of "The Nation" in which "The Party" exercises total control in a fictional world.

While the setting certainly lacks creativity, I was pleased to see that the plot and characters of the game improved as time passed. Orwell places the player as a worker for a state surveillence system looking for the perpetrator of a series of terrorist bombings. The player is tasked with reading various articles, profiles, and personal conversations and sending this information to the authorities within The Nation's government. This sounds more interesting than it plays out, however. In the beginning I was given a suspect who was very clearly not the bomber. I resented my superior for being so brainless for assuming they were responsible. While this suspect inevitably had some connections with people who actually did know more about the bombings, I was frustrated that I had to investigate the suspect in the first place. The gameplay also lacks for imagination. While I enjoyed reading some of the articles and the suspect's internet profiles, conversations, and e-mails, the text that you upload is already pre-determined. It ultimately boils down to a scavenger hunt. There are some choices to make things interesting. Sometimes you will have to chose between two pieces of data to upload to the authorities, as there may be conflicting data. Sometimes this decision is a moral one, and others it's more based around what the player things is more accuracte information. There are even a few times where uploading too much information will lead to unforeseen consequences. Regardless, for the most part the gameplay is very linear and will ultimately turn off many gamers. The gameplay gets more interesting in the final chapter when the uploads you can make are limited and the pressure is heightened, yet this improvement comes too little, too late.

Orwell is a game I want to love and there are moments of quality within. The general conclusion to the story was pulled off fairly well and there are consequences for chocies that many probably would not have anticipated being held accountable for. The characters and their interactions amongst each other are far more engaging than the uncreative setting. I hope for the sequel the developers be more bold with their setting, their message, and ultimately make the gameplay more interesting for a wider audience.

I received Orwell as part of a Humble Bundle and thought I'd give it a go. My play time is 6 hours and that's with a couple of hours when I just left the game open to answer a call or get the door. Overall it was a quick game.

I was interested in the concept of it, and they executed it very well. I was drawn into the characters, and their complex lives over the course of the 4 hours of play time. It's purely text based, but they still managed to bring these characters to life. Details like small misspellings, people overlapping each-other when they spoke over the messaging systems, and the way they lied to each-other, all make them feel like real people.

Ultimately you're faced with a choice at the end and, while I didn't play the last chapter twice to find out for sure, I'm pretty sure you can pick your ending based on your actions. 

If you're looking for something interesting but quick, and want to spend a few moments thinking about the implications of state surveillance programs, then pick this up. I am not a big fan of text-only games, but this did convince me to play through it to the end.  If you’re looking for action, graphics, or even voice acting, look elsewhere.

Orwell is a game where you step into the shoes of an "Investigator"; an individual specially chosen outside of the dystopian-like nation simply titled "The Nation" to interact with a big-brother type software that allows you to track and keep tabs on every single person in The Nation. You take control of yourself, your name, your info, you. You've been specially chosen for reasons unknown to yourself or anyone else, per the exception of a secretive few, to be hired at Orwell. Your new "Adviser", Symes, is going to show you the ropes of international and domestic espionage, only this time, you aren't taking down super villians or having a martini "shaken, not stirred" as per the classic spy movie or game, Orwell instead hits close to home....a little too close.

Orwell is a Story Rich, Dystopian, "Choices Matter" Indie game made by Osmotic Studios where you "Investigate the lives of citizens to find those responsible for a series of terror attacks. Information from the internet, personal communications and private files are all accessible to you. But, be warned, the information you supply will have consequences.". When Osmotic says that choices matter, they really do. You feel as if you're truly in this dystopian world, helping, or harming, The Nation's citizens. You get to look through countless web pages, trace and listen to countless phone calls, emails, text message and otherwise, even hack into citizen's computers or mobile phones to gain access to information stored on there, such as browsing history, photos, files, and even deleted files. 

For an example (spoiler free); You will be investigating certain citizens, and obviously need to find certain clues about them, their age, phone number, email address, face id, street info, parents, siblings, workplace, links to them from other sources, and you can even go as far as finding medical info from The Nation's hospitals. 

Now let's say I have a citizen I'm investigating, I can start with their relative name, go from there to their social media pages, find out their DOB, address, friends, maybe even mobile number. let's say I need to (or want to) take it further, I begin to suspect they're somehow a threat to The Nation. I can do a little research, Get in contact with friends, trace their calls and emails,  find out information that was never meant to be seen by hacking their computer by getting their PSI address or their IP address, or find ways into their workplace, or even goof off and research their background, what their favourite colour is, or who they're in a relationship with.

Orwell does an amazing job at immersing the investigator (you) into dystopian earth, into The Nation and it's surrounding countries, the citizens who inhabit them and even smaller things like a simple webpage for a local university or a humanitarian organization. Once I started the game, I honestly did not have high expectations nor did I think it was going to be something i was going to enjoy, since it just didn't look or seem like the type of game or genre that i liked, but once i started investigating and learning more about this country, it's citizens and the lore about this world I simply couldn't put it down. I played all the way through, read tons of webpages, information, emails and texts.

That being said, the game is roughly 3-4 hours long, maybe shorter if you (somehow) speedrun it, but if you really want to get immersed into this game world then it can take a lot longer.

[i] And that's not neccesarily a bad thing. [/i]

This is one of a only video game worlds and lore that I genuinly became interested in and invested in as time went on, it truly made me feel like I was impacting the citizens and world around me, mainly because I actually was.

One of the reasons this game resonated with me so much (and one of the reasons I am recommending it) is because in reality, this is not very dystopian. Things like this very well happen in real life and seem so real it's almost disturbing. The amount of dialogue in this game is astonishing, from everything to simple text messages to elaborate corporate emails, everything seems completely geniune, and feels that way too.

Orwell is a masterpeice at storytelling and really making the player truly become immersed and feel like there are consequences. Season 2 of Orwell is coming out sometime soon, and I WILL DEFINETLY be purchasing this game. I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes immersive game worlds, spy type games, choice matter games, or just mind-f*ck type games. Absolute great game. 10/10

Lately I've been finding myself bored with many games. I got through the motions without any real investment in what I've been playing... So, I decided to play something different. In comes Orwell. It's unlike any of the games I've toiled mundane hours hacking and slashing away in any random RPGs that I have on rotation. I've been engrossed in it for the past day getting familiar with the intricacies.

This is a different kind of spy game. One that might hit on reality a little closer than I'd like to think. Even more so if I was prone to ideas of the government watching our every move, which is why I'm an active VPN user. But I digress, Orwell is still just a game. A game where you play a data miner looking into the lives of who you might consider dangerous terrorists to a fictitious nation. I should mention there's quite a bit of reading. This isn't your mindless run and shoot game, or hide from the enemies and kill in secret game. It's not even graphically inspiring but the ideas and execution is solid. 

As you're uncovering terrorists and their plots you get deeper into the lives of those you think are involved and have to feed information into the Orwell system to determine their threat level. The game has you scouring through newspapers, blogs, and social media feeds to gain as much information as possible. It would be overwhelming if the interface wasn't so simple to navigate. 

While progression in the game is pretty linear you do have the ability to impact significant events based on what you choose to feed into the system. There is also an abundance of conflicting information that you will have to make judgement calls on what you want to submit. Orwell do a good job highlighting these inconsistencies. The only thing I might have qualms with is there's no "undo" feature. So if you do happen to make a mistake and upload something you'd rather not you don't have a second chance to fix or update your mistakes. The system for all it's abilities has a permanent function. Like most things once it's out there it's there for good. 

In all Orwell is an engaging game where you play big brother and stop terrorists a different way. It's got a solid story and characters and an easy to use interface. It may or may not resemble some truth to life but in the immortal words of Harold Finch "It's not paranoia if they really are out to get you" and in this game you're out to get everyone.

Orwell is a story-based game in almost the purest sense. The interactions are clicking and dragging highlighted blurbs, pictures, and quotes, and these submissions can color the way these people are treated throughout the game. Going through the story is the real goal of the game, and revealing the how everything ties together was definitely worth a couple of playthroughs. 

For a game with next to no animation, it used collections of static images and statements that still forms a full picture of their character, flaws and all. In fact, only the intro has animated characters of any sort, but given the nature of the game it just makes more sense to use static images like how we use avatars on our own proviles. If I had to describe games with a similar sort of style, I'd say something like Mirror's Edge or the Abstergo stuff in Assassin's Creed: sharp edges and smooth lines, that kind of sleek that suggests futuristic but clinical.

All in all, had a highly intriguing time, would surveille again.

omg i immediately got sucked into this game. it just pulls you in with its twists and turns. idk how this is done tradiitonally so i'm gunna wing it.

genre: it's a slow-paced political/espionage thriller about working for the wrong side. for some reason, i was reminded of counterfeit monkey in how the world felt in this game.

story-telling: best part of the game. it's all told through reading articles, websites, medical records, phone calls, private emails. this game got me feeling equal parts paranoid (about my own online data) and guilty (about how obedient i was in being an oppressive surveillance tool). it just kinda... slowly built up. there were twists and turns galore!

actual story: draws pretty heavily on the 1984 book in terms of central themes, but i feel like it definitely updates it to the present. some parts were pretty hokey and implausible, but eh. but some parts were actually kinda scary and real. idk, there are fears i have when i go about the internet and this game left quite an impression on those fears.

visuals: pretty serviceable. probably the only thing that annoyed me was how small the window got as your network grew. but i enjoyed the geometric art and the almost facebook-like interface.

gameplay: it's actually pretty simple yet also kinda inventive. you feed an advisor "datachunks" that help their investigation. they can talk to you, but you can't talk to them. it makes you feel like an alienated observer almost, except you're definitely not because you're basically trying to crush opposition to the government. reminded me of the miller obedience studies a lot, idk. (Edit: Okay, i played this game three times overall to get all achievements. It was pretty fun! I spent a lot of time trying to figure everything out and consider all the thematic elements!!

overall: i feel like as a work of art, it's 9/10. i would definitely show this game to people and it's left a real impression on me. put this game with the likes of this war of mine, papers please, and counterfeit monkey. however, just like those games (except counterfeit monkey), when you play this game you're either on the edge of your seat with your nails between your teeth or you're feeling like an office drone trying to put these details together for your boss. this game isn't really something you play so you can have "fun" as such. it's an experience.

I didn't think much of the orwellian gimmick after the first few interactions with the system, which is something I thought I'd fault the game for, but in fact I think it's better this way because the insidious nature of the surveillance at hand feels ickier when you suddenly realise what it is you're actually doing. So in the end, I quite thoroughly enjoyed the story and the message, and I'm looking forward to the sequel.

Orwell is one of those games that you can't really describe to anyone based on other games. Is it a simulation? A puzzle? The first of a whole new category? I wouldn't go as far as the latter, but one thing's for sure: it's intriguing. You think you've got it all figured out and then some other clue pops up that ruins your entire theory. So you keep playing.

At first it feels like the game is holding your hand the entire time and, really, any interactivity is there just to give you something to do while the story unfolds before you. But if you have the patience, you end up realizing that you needed all that hand holding to prepare you for the real deal.

And it's hard. And easy as well. Confusingly so. But the most difficult part for me was the ending. Not because the game mechanics were too hard for me to master, but because of ethics. After all, that's all the game is about, as you'll see if you try it.

And you most definitely should!

In Orwell, you are the human filter on a state-run mass-surveillance tool called Orwell, hunting the perpetrators of a series of terror attacks. It plays a lot more like a piece of interactive fiction than a game - I've deliberately chosen "interactive fiction" over "choose your own adventure" as I'm not sure there are too many alternate routes to take. That shouldn't be taken as criticism, either - Orwell is really engaging, if a little slow at times.

[b]The good[/b]
[list]
[*]Story - The story is good and is told well as you sort through web pages, phone/text/email conversations and sift through your targets' computers and mobile devices.
[*]Duration - Orwell doesn't outstay it's welcome - it's pretty much the right length. There were a couple of points where I had the feeling things were about to start dragging, but then something happened and picked the pace up again.
[/list]

[b]The bad[/b]
[list]
[*]The tagging process - You have to drag and drop datachunks to the appropriate targets. This makes sense, but Orwell tells you who they'll be tagged to. As your number of targets increases, switching to the right one feels a bit pointless. If the system will only allow the datachunk to be tagged to that target and you’re telling me who it has to be tagged to, just tag it to them - don't make me switch around!
[/list]

This is an interactive fiction game about how a government's attempt to protect the nation can easily spiral out of control. You are placed in the role of the investigator tasked with finding the perpetrators of a terrorist attack. You control Orwell, a government spy system that gives you the power to investigate the private internet lives of suspected targets. Though the guided storyline keeps you on track, the information you release or withold from the government will affect the storyline's progression and most prominently, the ending. A player that is not paying close attention to the story can mistakenly pass along bad or misleading information to the officials. The game itself does have some technical issues that can frustrate new players, but most solutions can be found online. Very enjoyable concept and story, highly recommended.

You play as an investigator parsing through information using a big brother system. The system finds almost everything important, and you have to decide if its relevant, correct, or out of context. Some information is not highlighted, but will resolve conflicting information. This game mostly reading, but you are given direction and information that you are going in the right direction (the end, you can be wrong). It plays like out like you are on the show 24, trying to solve a mystery and stop it, but you are responsible for solving the mystery. Incredibly rewarding if you get it right.

Certainly the best game I have played in the last time. Highly recommended.

I got this game from Humble Monthly and wasn't expecting much. Then I found out this game lives up to its name.
Orwell has quite a few tense moments when you discover shocking revelations with your surveillance capabilities, and sometimes you find yourself reviewing your past 'discoveries' to reveal greater plots and conspiracies.
I find that the greatest feature of Orwell is its story, and the way it makes you reflect about the hypocrisy and arrogance necessary to make such a surveillance system.

When you finish this game you will never look upon the idea of 'Big Brother' in the same way.

About the mechanics and graphics I find the controls easy to use and that the graphics do not detract from the story.

Unfortunately, it seems short (although with plenty of content in that short time) and if you are spoiled or already played the game before you already know about the whole story and do not have to search very hard to find trustworthy information (after all, you already know what happens)
Phenomenal story line, gameplay was addicting and immersive

The premise is you are the thought police. You read social media, email, listen in on phone calls, etc.

BE CAREFUL WHAT YOU UPLOAD because you may accidentally get people killed, by either failing to prevent catastrophic events or cornering someone who's not going down without a fight.

I wouldn't call this game amazing by any stretch of the imagination.

You're heralded as an "investigator" but the game is so on rails that you never get to make any decisions. You're forced to choose highlighted pieces of information from simulated webpages in a very set order, which makes the game totally linear.

You are basically just reading a story and clicking on certain sentences and phrases when prompted.

The game is fairly original in it's visual presentation, and the "big brother" aesthetic is probably why people are giving it positive reviews. I just can't recommend it though.
